analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: October FOMC Preview: Hiking at a Slower Pace
key_insights: GS reads FOMC comments since September as a compromise to raise the funds rate every other meeting. The FOMC is set to skip a hike at its October meeting and is likely to deliver a second and final hike in December, in line with the GS forecast.

The Fed's hawkish pivot has driven a 30bp tightening in the GS Financial Conditions Index since September. The index had been little changed earlier in 2026 because higher rates were offset by higher stocks and narrower credit spreads.

The 30bp FCI tightening is only a bit more than is usually associated with one 25bp hike and much less than is usually associated with the four hikes the market has priced. GS therefore expects the FOMC to see it as neither excessive nor a replacement for further hikes.

The key October question is how the statement modifies the sentence on the September hike. GS thinks the Committee might adapt Vice Chair Jefferson's language: 'Any further adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate to support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal will depend on trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.'

If Chairman Warsh finds the Jefferson-style language too close to past forward guidance, GS says the alternative would be to say nothing about the policy outlook, a bigger departure from past Fed practice.

GS does not expect significant new information from the press conference. Strong support for hiking every other meeting implies a high bar to deviate through year-end, and Warsh did not hint at the slower pace at his September press conference, so he may again leave that to others. Warsh could give an initial update on his task forces, but final conclusions are probably too early.

An every-other-meeting pace in 2027 would put the next hike consideration in March, with five more months of inflation data. GS does not expect a March hike because it expects inflation to improve as tariff, energy shock and AI price effects fade.
GS estimates that tariffs, the Iran energy shock and the mismeasured part of AI price pressures account for all of core PCE inflation's current 1.1pp overshoot of the 2% target.

A March hike is possible if inflation runs worse than GS expects. The clearest upside risk is oil futures above the GS forecast on concerns about further Middle East conflict. If oil follows the futures, core PCE rises another 0.1pp by March and the headline forecast about 0.4pp.

On tariffs, GS finds incremental passthrough from earlier rounds is essentially over, so year-on-year inflation should keep falling on base effects. Replacement of tariffs overturned by the courts should have only a modest impact.
On energy, GS estimates higher oil prices and refined product spreads have lifted core PCE inflation by 0.3pp so far and would add 0.1-0.15pp more under its baseline oil forecast.

On AI, GS expects the impact on year-over-year core PCE inflation to peak over the next few months and fall meaningfully in 2027 as memory and computer price growth slow. Month-to-month memory price effects have been erratic, so near-term uncertainty remains.

Prices-received components of business surveys have risen substantially in manufacturing but remain at normal levels in services. Prolonged pressure could raise the risk of a larger 'January effect' as firms pass on costs with start-of-year price increases.

GS suspects some FOMC participants share its view that the economy is not overheated and that the supply-shock overshoot must largely be waited out, so they may prefer to limit the size of the hiking cycle. Concerns about growth or employment would likely end hikes.

Market pricing has removed one hike since end-September and now peaks near 4.55% in fall 2027, implying just under three more hikes for four in total. GS baseline and probability-weighted paths are less hawkish because GS expects only two hikes and cuts later.

risk_factors: Oil futures above GS forecasts on Middle East conflict risk is the clearest upside risk to inflation.
A larger January effect from start-of-year price increases could raise inflation prints before the March meeting.
Inflation could broaden beyond manufacturing, where prices-received survey components have jumped, into services.
Higher energy prices could erode real income and weigh on consumer spending, which would likely end hikes.
A more substantial tightening in financial conditions than seen so far could end hikes.
AI-related memory price pass-through is erratic month to month.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 shows changes in the GS US FCI since January 1, 2026, and the peak Fed funds rate priced for 2027. The text says the FCI tightened 30bp since September.
Exhibit 3 shows tariffs, the Iran energy shock and the mismeasured part of AI price pressures accounting for all of core PCE's 1.1pp overshoot of the 2% target.
Exhibit 4 shows the energy shock has boosted core PCE inflation by 0.3pp and will add 0.1-0.15pp under the GS oil forecast, or 0.25pp if oil follows the higher futures curve.

tension_points.bull_case: Market pricing implies four hikes in total with a peak near 4.55% in fall 2027. Oil futures above GS forecasts, a larger January effect and a possible March hike would support more tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: GS expects only two hikes, with inflation easing as tariff, energy and AI effects fade, and cuts later. Growth or employment concerns would end hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A March 2027 hike or oil following the higher futures curve (adding 0.1pp to core PCE by March) would challenge the GS two-hike baseline.
